title: Review: Titrations and solution calculations; Organic practical techniques; Tests for ions; Aldehydes and ketones
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT07#t2 term and clue written for the game; PT07#t4 term and clue written for the game; OR17a#t4 term and clue written for the game; OR17a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AM08b#N.5, OR17a#N.9, OR27#N.14, PT07#N.3, AM08b#N.10, OR17a#N.12, OR27#N.11, PT07#N.6, AM08b#N.3, OR17a#N.6, OR27#N.4, PT07#N.14a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anion
items.clue: The negative particle in a salt, such as SO₄²⁻ or CO₃²⁻.

items.label: Barium chloride
items.clue: Solution added after dilute HCl; gives a white precipitate with sulfate.

items.label: Hydroxynitrile
items.clue: Product of adding HCN across C=O, e.g. CH₃CH(OH)CN; the chain gains one carbon.

items.label: Carbonyl
items.clue: The C=O group, around which the arrangement is trigonal planar with angles of about 120°.

questions.stem: 10.0 cm³ of vinegar is diluted to 100.0 cm³ in a volumetric flask. A 25.0 cm³ portion needs 20.75 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O. What was the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar, in mol dm⁻³?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.02075 = 2.075 × 10⁻³ mol = n(acid) in the portion. 2.075 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0830 diluted; × 10 = 0.830 in the vinegar.

questions.stem: In the mechanism for the reaction of propanone with cyanide, where does the first curly arrow start and end?

options.text: From the lone pair on the N of CN⁻ to the carbonyl carbon
From the lone pair on the C of CN⁻ to the carbonyl carbon
From the C=O π bond to the C of CN⁻
From a lone pair on the carbonyl O to H⁺

questions.explanation: The cyanide carbon's lone pair forms the new C–C bond to the δ+ carbonyl carbon.

questions.stem: A student makes 1-bromobutane (bp 102 °C, density 1.27 g cm⁻³) from butan-1-ol (bp 118 °C). The crude product contains water, acid and some unreacted alcohol. Which purification is best?

options.text: Keep the upper layer, since organic liquids float on water; dry it, then distil at 100–104 °C.
Keep the lower layer; wash with NaHCO₃(aq), venting; dry; distil at 100–104 °C.
Dry the crude mixture with anhydrous MgSO₄ first, then wash it with water and distil.
Keep the lower layer, dry it, then collect everything that distils below 118 °C.

questions.explanation: Density puts the product at the bottom; NaHCO₃ removes acid; the salt removes water; distilling near 102 °C leaves the alcohol (118 °C) behind.

questions.stem: Which result shows that a solid contains ammonium ions?

options.text: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added; a gas forms that turns limewater milky.
It is warmed with NaOH(aq); a gas forms that turns damp red litmus paper blue.
NaOH(aq) is added to its solution; a white precipitate forms that stays on warming.
Its solution turns damp blue litmus paper red, and no gas forms on warming.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ ions remove H⁺ from NH₄⁺, releasing ammonia, the only common alkaline gas.

questions.stem: An impure sample of magnesium oxide, an insoluble base, is analysed by back titration. MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l). Assume the impurities do not react with acid. 0.400 g of the sample is added to 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl (excess). The leftover acid needs 14.30 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. What is the percentage by mass of MgO in the sample? (Aᵣ: O 16.0, Mg 24.3)
Hex-5-en-2-one, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂COCH₃, has a C=C bond and a C=O bond. It is warmed with NaBH₄(aq). What is the organic product?

options.text: Hex-5-en-2-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃
Hexan-2-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃
Hexan-2-one, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂COCH₃
Hex-5-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH

questions.explanation: H⁻ is a nucleophile. It attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O. The non-polar, electron-rich C=C does not attract it.

questions.stem: Pure aspirin melts at 136 °C. A student's recrystallised aspirin melts over the range 126–131 °C. What does this show?

options.text: It is pure: melting below 136 °C shows that no aspirin decomposed.
It is impure: the impurity must be a substance that melts at 126 °C.
It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and widen the range.
It is pure: every pure solid melts gradually over a range of about 5 °C.

questions.explanation: Low and broad (126–131 °C) means impure. Recrystallise again and re-measure.

questions.stem: A student adds barium chloride solution to a solution of an unknown sodium salt, without adding acid first. A white precipitate forms. Why can the student not yet conclude that sulfate ions are present?

options.text: Barium chloride gives a white precipitate with every negative ion.
The white solid could be sodium chloride crystallising out of the mixture.
The solid could be barium carbonate, which acid would have prevented.
Barium ions react with water to form a white barium hydroxide precipitate.

questions.explanation: BaCO₃ is also white and insoluble. Dilute HCl first removes carbonate as CO₂, so a white precipitate after acidifying must be BaSO₄.

questions.stem: In a back titration, an insoluble carbonate is added to excess hydrochloric acid, and the leftover acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide. Which amount equals the moles of HCl that reacted with the carbonate?

options.text: The moles of NaOH used in the titration of the leftover acid
The moles of HCl added to the solid at the very start
The moles of HCl added minus the moles of NaOH used in the titre
Half the moles of NaOH used in the titration of the leftover acid

questions.explanation: HCl reacts 1 : 1 with NaOH, so n(NaOH) = acid left over. Subtract it from the acid added to get the acid the carbonate used.

questions.stem: Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, is reduced. Reagent: NaBH₄(aq). What is the organic product?

options.text: Butan-1-ol
Butane
Butan-2-ol
Butanoic acid

questions.explanation: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃. A ketone gives a secondary alcohol.

questions.stem: A student wants to make propanal from propan-1-ol using acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Which method gives the most propanal?

options.text: Heat the alcohol under reflux with excess oxidant for an hour, then distil the mixture.
Heat the alcohol under reflux with a small amount of oxidant, then distil.
Distil the alcohol first, then add the oxidant to the distillate.
Add the oxidant slowly to warm alcohol and distil off propanal as it forms.

questions.explanation: Propanal (bp 48 °C) boils lower than propan-1-ol (97 °C), so it distils out before it can be oxidised further.

questions.stem: A garden-centre sack of white fertiliser crystals has lost its label. It could be ammonium sulfate, ammonium carbonate, ammonium chloride or potassium sulfate. Which pair of results shows it is ammonium sulfate?

options.text: Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate that fizzes and dissolves when dilute HCl is added.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives no alkaline gas; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq) gives a white precipitate.
